doc.title: Tom Scott interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 1, 2022 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Scoring to the finished picture and psychological scenes
summary: He prefers to see a near-final film as a first audience member and enjoys scenes of psychological drama.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: Regarding themes for the subsequent shows you did after “Dan August,” music sometimes can convey emotions and sometimes music is just music. So was your task to read the description of what this show’s going to be about, maybe about the characters you know, it’s a cop but he’s got marital trouble, he’s got a young kid etcetera, and how much did the music you were trying to write reflect the story?

Right. Great question. Well obviously — needless to say — music for films and television is a highly subjective matter. And so the good news for me, for me as a composer, is I get to see the film for the first time when it’s basically complete except for the music. I cannot tell you how many times I’ve said I don’t want to read the script, I don’t want to see it halfway edited, because I want to see as close as you can get to the final product as possible before you show it to me. Now that’s not always possible. Sometimes I had to, you know, see it an incompleted movie or a movie that was still to be

final edited, and of course I was just reminded of a — I don’t know what it was, years ago, some movie, a movie of the week for television. So I’m busy writing and the director calls and he says, “Listen, Tom, we’ve made some cuts in this one scene but it won’t affect you.” Like hell it won’t affect me. I didn’t say that back, but that’s what I’m thinking. Let me be the judge of whether it affects me or not because it could change everything. It could change the whole tone of it. But back to the question, I like to respond, as I say, when I’m seeing the final or closest to final version. I want to respond as the audience does. I’m the first like audience. So the music should, you know, should work kind of in terms of the audience’s expectations. In other words is it just literally like a chase? Somebody chasing somebody? Or is there some psychologic — I love, by the way, scenes where there’s some psychological drama. Not just what’s going on action- wise on the screen but what’s going on in someone’s head. You know? They’re about to murder somebody but they’re not sure whether they want to do it or not, but they’re having this normal conversation with the person who may be the victim, and you’ve got to play their thinking — “Oh I want to get this person” — but you have to do it, you know, that’s really fun. You know the action scenes, you know I mean they’ve got to be done. But you asked about whether knowing the character’s full story — it doesn’t necessarily matter. It only matters in terms of what this scene is that we’re looking at and what’s going on there and do these character elements, do they play into this scene or not? And if they do then obviously you’ve got to take that into consideration.
